title: The cravat: how Croatian soldiers gave us the tie
hook: The necktie owes its name to Croatian soldiers in 17th-century France.
peek: When Croatian soldiers fighting for France arrived in Paris in the 1600s, they wore knotted scarves at the neck. Parisians copied the look and named it after them. The word cravat comes from Croat.
lede: In the 1600s, Croatian mercenaries serving the French crown wore knotted cloths around their necks. Fashionable Parisians copied the style, and the French called it a cravate, from the word for a Croat. That word spread across Europe, and the cravat became the ancestor of the modern necktie. Croatia still marks Cravat Day every year on 18 October.

bullets.text: Croatia gets the name, not the invention. Roman soldiers wore a neck scarf called a focale, and some figures in China's Terracotta Army have cloth at the neck too.
In Regency London, the dandy Beau Brummell made tying a starched cravat into an art. Getting the knot exactly right could reportedly take a long time and several spoiled cloths.
In 1999 two Cambridge physicists, Thomas Fink and Yong Mao, used mathematics to count the possible tie knots of a reasonable size. They found 85, and later work by others counted far more.
The everyday narrow knot is usually linked to a London club of carriage drivers or to the reins of a four-horse coach. Nobody is sure which, so treat both as likely stories.
The cravat is one of many everyday things named for where they supposedly came from. The croissant has a similar story, with Austrian roots under a French name.
By the late 1800s the cravat had narrowed into the long tie and the bow tie. The bow tie found a permanent home with evening wear, including the jacket named after a town in New York.
